description: We are a passionate, energetic, disciplined, and collaborative team united by our curiosity about space, astronomy, physics, software, and technology. We value teamwork, creativity, learning, and staying committed to our goals. We enjoy exploring new ideas, solving problems together, and channeling our curiosity into meaningful projects.
summary: ARESIGHT is an interactive, browser-based decision-support tool for planning human surface traverses on Mars. It is built on NASA data: MGS MOLA elevation and slope, TES and Viking layers for dust, rock abundance, thermal inertia and albedo, and a radiation model scaled from Curiosity RAD measurements. Users choose a region, crew, mobility mode (on foot, unpressurized or pressurized rover), dust opacity and solar particle events. ARESIGHT then computes three alternative routes and rates each with a green, yellow or red safety assessment covering slope, radiation, loose dust, rocky terrain and consumables, including a 20% reserve. The challenge is that crews must choose safe, efficient routes far from Earth, on a planet where data quality varies from place to place. ARESIGHT makes this uncertainty explicit: every result shows how far it can be trusted. Users can also explore the terrain in 3D, through the astronaut’s helmet visor or in VR, and simulate the link with Earth. This matters because better traverse planning protects astronauts and helps future missions reach the most valuable science sites.
details:
ARESIGHT: Project Description

What it is and how it works
Mars Traverse Planner is a browser-based mission planning tool for walking or driving across the surface of Mars. The user picks a region (for example the Milankovic Crater robot landing site, the Noctis Landing base with four sorties, or the InSight landing site), a mode of travel (on foot, unpressurized rover, or pressurized rover on a multi-day traverse), a crew, and the equipment carried. The system then plans three alternative routes:

  • Route A: shortest distance
  • Route B: lowest slope and terrain risk
  • Route C: most science opportunities

For each route it calculates oxygen, battery, water and CO2 use against a 20% reserve, maximum slope, rock density, soft-soil risk, communication coverage, radiation, and the effects of dust opacity and solar particle events. A decision engine scores each route and recommends one, with plain reasons (“resources insufficient for the round trip”, “steepest section 22°”). Every result is color-coded green, yellow or red, together with an indicator of how far the underlying data can be trusted: HiRISE-class (0.25–0.5 m/pixel), CTX-class (about 6 m/pixel), or low resolution. The tool does not hide data gaps.

The app has several linked views:

  • Map and route: layered maps (elevation, rocks, temperature, minerals, water, radiation, dust, thermal inertia, confidence) with a traverse animation.
  • Astronaut and tablet: a simulated astronaut tablet and an exploration robot that can take samples.
  • Safety and decision engine: resource gauges, hazard assessment, and a copyable mission report.
  • 3D terrain and helmet visor: a 3D terrain view and an astronaut’s-eye view that also opens in a VR headset (WebXR).
  • Planet 3D: a Sun-to-Mars flight with real planetary positions.
  • Comms: an Earth and base link with realistic delay.
  • Data sets: users can upload their own layers and science sites.

Benefits

  • Turns scattered Mars datasets into one clear, explainable go/no-go decision.
  • Compares routes by three different goals (speed, safety, science) instead of one “best” path.
  • Shows honest uncertainty, so planners know where the data is thin.
  • Works for students, educators, mission-concept teams and the public. It needs no installation, runs in one HTML file, and is available in English.
  • Lets users bring their own data (images or JSON) and their own region, so it is reusable beyond the built-in missions.

Intended impact
The project aims to make Mars surface mission planning understandable and accessible. It helps people see why a route is safe or risky, and it supports early-stage mission design and education. It also shows the value of combining open planetary data with transparent decision logic. The planned research steps it lists (ground-penetrating radar, neutron spectrometer, weather station, dosimeter) point to real instruments flown on Curiosity, Perseverance and TGO, so the tool connects directly to current Mars exploration.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript only, in a single self-contained file.
  • Graphics: HTML5 Canvas for maps and charts. Three.js (WebGL) for 3D terrain, the astronaut, the rover, the robot and the planet view. WebXR for VR headsets.
  • Algorithms: A* pathfinding with a binary heap and a different cost function per route. Line-of-sight communication coverage, slope derived from elevation, and resource and risk models. Procedural noise (fractal Brownian motion) for generated near terrain and rocks.
  • Orbital and flight physics: Keplerian orbital elements (JPL) and the IAU 2015 Mars rotation model. Hohmann transfer and Kepler equation solving. Simulated Earth ascent and Mars entry, descent and landing (parachute and powered descent).
  • Data: Real MOLA elevation data for distant terrain. Published slope, rock and thermal inertia statistics, and HiRISE/CTX/THEMIS/TES-based layers, for the regions.
  • Hardware: Any modern computer or phone browser. An optional VR headset.

Creativity

  • It joins mission planning, physics simulation, a 3D first-person experience and a solar-system view in one tool.
  • Its trust indicator (green, yellow, red, plus data resolution) shows uncertainty next to every result.
  • Astronauts, rover and robot are 3D models generated entirely in code, with no external assets.
  • Planning, rehearsal and experience happen in one place: plan the route, then walk it in first person or in VR.

Factors considered

  • Safety: resource reserve, slope limits, rock fields, soft ground that could trap wheels, radiation and solar particle events, dust opacity, and loss of communications.
  • Scientific value: water, minerals and geology scored along each route.
  • Data quality: clear separation of measured data from generated or simulated values. Health values and robot scan results are labeled as simulated.
  • Accessibility: one file, no installation, light and dark themes, mobile-friendly layout.
  • Extensibility: custom regions, custom layers, importable and exportable points and routes.Mars Mission: Infrastructure, Data Mapping, and Landing Safety Summary
    The primary challenges in the Arcadia Planitia and Milankovic Crater regions—located at high northern latitudes (54.4° N) on Mars—include the risk of heavy vehicles sinking into surface dust, the potential for rocket exhaust to instantly melt shallow subsurface ice (leading to ground collapse), and insufficient solar energy due to the high latitude.
    To overcome these obstacles and ensure the safety of human-related operations, the mission employs autonomous, nuclear-powered robots equipped with sintering technology. Powered by nuclear units—allowing them to operate continuously, independent of sunlight—these robots use high-power lasers or microwaves to heat Martian regolith to temperatures exceeding 1,000°C, transforming it into a hard, ceramic-like rock layer. This process is primarily used to construct a robust landing pad capable of withstanding the intense heat and pressure generated by rocket exhaust, thereby preventing the melting of the ground and the ejection of debris.
    Furthermore, the robots sinter and harden two specific strips—aligned with the intended wheel tracks—extending toward the northeast of the crater. During this construction phase, the robots utilize Ground-Penetrating Radar (GPR), LiDAR sensors, and ground-pressure measurement tools to collect high-precision data, including 3D terrain topography, temperature profiles, and ice-layer thickness. These digital maps are then fed directly into the autopilot systems of the heavy rovers arriving later, enabling them to navigate to the crater floor in a fully autonomous and secure manner, without the risk of becoming bogged down in the regolith or overturning.
